Fake World Assets (FWA) is an incredibly interesting mechanic + worth observing

but my concern is what happens when the FWA price reverses…

Right now the reflexivity works in its favour:

Activity → FWA rewards → higher $ value of those rewards → better LP returns → more attractive NFTs deposited → better gacha experience → more activity

The problem is that same flywheel can spin backwards (see diagram):

FWA price ↓ → depositor rewards worth less → LP returns compress → fewer attractive NFTs enter the pool → pool quality deteriorates → gacha EV / excitement falls → fewer spins → lower fees → lower ETH yield for depositors → lower protocol revenue → less potential buyback demand → FWA price ↓

The 15-day bootstrap makes this particularly interesting, with 30% of supply distributed between depositors and purchasers before the model transitions towards protocol-revenue-funded buybacks

The real test for FWA therefore isn’t whether the incentive design can bootstrap activity, it’s whether that activity remains once the value of the subsidy falls

Is the protocol attractive without FWA incentives?

If yes, FWA is an accelerator for an underlying economic engine

If no, FWA is subsidising activity and the reflexivity that made the launch so powerful can work just as aggressively in reverse

Death spiral backstop solution: 

Direct a portion of protocol revenue to LPs in ETH rather than routing it all through FWA buybacks, creating a token-price-independent yield floor that keeps quality NFTs deposited even if FWA falls

"If you're in crypto, pivot to AI."

I used to hear versions of this, and it's the wrong way to think about the world. It's zero sum, scarcity thinking.

Crypto is a general purpose technology. It's infrastructure, the same way electricity or the internet is infrastructure. It doesn't compete with the next big thing, because it underpins it. It's an *and*, not an *or*.

AI being a megatrend takes nothing away from crypto. If anything, it makes crypto more important.

What if the biggest market signal this week was not Brent briefly breaking $100—but what rose alongside it?

Why did uranium, gold, silver and copper strengthen while the Nasdaq fell?

Are investors beginning to price a world in which energy, metals and food security matter more than ever?

I think they are.

MARKET UPDATE

Brent gained almost 10% for the week and briefly closed above $100. The diplomatic pause is encouraging, but traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains extremely limited while the Red Sea is also under threat.

My main concern for the broader markets is simple:

Oil → inflation → higher interest rates for longer.

Despite this risk-off environment, several hard assets performed well: gold gained 1.4%, silver 4.7% and copper around 1.6%. I see this as another sign that capital is increasingly looking for scarce, essential commodities.

China hoarding gold is a tell.

Uranium also showed resilience. $URA and $URNM gained around 3%, spot remained near $86/lb and the June long-term price reached $97/lb. The July indicator, due in early August, will be very interesting.

Utilities appear willing to pay a substantial premium to spot to secure future supply.

The Middle East conflict is not yet a direct uranium supply shock, although disruption to sulphur markets could eventually affect sulphuric acid availability and uranium production costs.

More importantly, the conflict strengthens the strategic case for nuclear power. Nuclear fuel can be stockpiled for years, and reactors can continue producing reliable electricity without depending on daily tanker traffic through vulnerable shipping lanes.

I am also increasingly bullish on copper. Chinese imports are strong, inventories are falling, and new grids, nuclear plants, AI data centres and defence infrastructure will all require enormous quantities of the metal.

Potash fits the same security theme: increasingly fragile fertilizer markets should enhance the strategic value of large, reliable North American resources.

Next week, $CCJ Cameco will release its Q2 results on July 31, followed by its investor conference call and webcast at 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time.

I will be listening closely to what Cameco says about contracting, utility demand and the uranium market—and I expect the overall message to be nothing short of extremely bullish.
